entries.name: Shōgatsu (Japanese New Year)
entries.capsule: Japan's New Year on January 1; in Minnesota, marked in homes and at the Japan America Society's Shinnenkai party.
entries.dateRule: January 1 on the Gregorian calendar, with observances over the first days of January. Minnesota community parties (Shinnenkai) are set by organizers each year.

dates.source: Fixed Gregorian date (no opened Minnesota page states it)
Fixed Gregorian date (no opened Minnesota page states it)
Fixed Gregorian date (no opened Minnesota page states it)

entries.whatItMarks: The start of the new year, Japan's most important family holiday.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: The Japan America Society of Minnesota describes an annual Shinnenkai (New Year celebration) with cultural performances, Japanese food and a raffle; no 2026 or 2027 date was found. The Twin Cities JACL's chapter history recalls a mochi (rice cake) fundraiser that sold more than 1,000 pounds.

entries.name: Day of Remembrance (Executive Order 9066)
entries.capsule: February 19 marks the 1942 order that led to Japanese Americans' forced removal; the Twin Cities JACL holds an annual program.
entries.dateRule: February 19 each year, the date Executive Order 9066 was signed in 1942. Minnesota programs may fall on or near that date.

dates.source: MNopedia states the order was issued February 19, 1942; Twin Cities JACL held its program Feb. 19, 2026

entries.whatItMarks: The signing of Executive Order 9066 on February 19, 1942, which led to the forced removal and incarceration of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: The Twin Cities JACL hosts a yearly program with film and discussion. In 2026, about 100 people attended a Feb. 19 screening of One Fighting Irishman with a panel; in 2025 it was held Feb. 16 at the Minnesota History Center with MNHS.

minnesotaEvents.name: Twin Cities JACL Day of Remembrance: screening of One Fighting Irishman
minnesotaEvents.place: Twin Cities (venue not stated in opened sources)

entries.name: Obon
entries.capsule: Buddhist season for welcoming and honoring ancestors, with dances and lanterns; celebrated in Minnesota at temple services and a large Como Park festival.
entries.dateRule: Mid-July or mid-August depending on region and temple in Japan. Minnesota dates are set by each organizer; see the separate Como Park Obon Festival entry.
entries.whatItMarks: Remembrance of ancestors, whose spirits are said to return home for a few days and are guided back with lanterns.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: The Twin Cities Buddhist Sangha (Jodo Shinshu) holds its own Obon; the JACL newsletter listed it for July 29, 2026, a date not confirmed by the sangha. The public Como Park Japanese Obon Festival is in August (separate entry).

minnesotaEvents.name: Twin Cities Buddhist Church Obon Festival (as listed)
minnesotaEvents.organizerDates: Listed as July 29, 2026, in the Twin Cities JACL calendar; not confirmed by the sangha

sources.title: Obon Festival, Como Park Zoo and Conservatory
Twin Cities Buddhist Sangha 80th anniversary, Buddhist Churches of America

entries.name: Como Park Japanese Obon Festival
entries.capsule: Minnesota's largest Japan-related festival: taiko, dance, food and floating lanterns at Como Park in St. Paul each August.
entries.dateRule: One Sunday in mid-August, announced by Como Park Zoo and Conservatory with its partners.
entries.whatItMarks: Japan's Obon season of honoring ancestors, adapted as a public cultural festival.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: On the Marjorie McNeely Conservatory grounds, 3 to 9 p.m., with taiko, koto, shakuhachi, dance, martial arts, food and vendors, a Bon Odori dance, and lantern lighting at about 8 p.m. in the Japanese Garden and Frog Pond. Produced by Como, the Japan America Society of Minnesota and the Saint Paul-Nagasaki Sister City Committee. Advance tickets only in 2026 ($8 adults). The Twin Cities JACL counted 8,530 attendees in 2026.

minnesotaEvents.name: Como Park Japanese Obon Festival 2026
minnesotaEvents.place: Marjorie McNeely Conservatory grounds, 1225 Estabrook Dr., St. Paul

entries.name: Minnesota Japanese American Veterans Graveside Decorating
alsoKnownAs: Japanese American veterans memorial, Fort Snelling
entries.capsule: Before Memorial Day, families decorate the graves of Minnesota's Japanese American veterans at Fort Snelling National Cemetery.
entries.dateRule: A Saturday in mid-May before Memorial Day, set by the Twin Cities JACL.
entries.whatItMarks: Service of Japanese American veterans, including Military Intelligence Service linguists trained in Minnesota.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: Flowers are picked up at Fort Snelling National Cemetery and placed on the graves of 101 Japanese American veterans buried there; 35 more buried elsewhere were also honored in 2026. In 2024 a memorial program drew Gen. Paul Nakasone and his father.

minnesotaEvents.name: Minnesota Japanese American Veterans Graveside Decorating
minnesotaEvents.place: Fort Snelling National Cemetery, 7601 34th Ave. S., Minneapolis

sources.title: Minnesotans honor the state's Japanese American veterans, MPR News

entries.name: Ireichō (Book of Names) at Historic Fort Snelling
entries.capsule: In October 2026 the traveling book naming over 125,000 incarcerated Japanese Americans visited Fort Snelling for name-stamping.
entries.dateRule: One-time Minnesota stop of a national tour.
entries.whatItMarks: Each person incarcerated in World War II, honored by name.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: Three-day stop at the Plank Museum and Visitor Center, a restored barracks of the language school, with MNHS and the Twin Cities JACL; visitors stamped names, and Densho scanned family materials and recorded interviews.
